ns2:section.sectionText: The University of Illinois is a land-grant university, which means that land was given to its founders, free of charge, in order to create a university that educated and uplifted the residents of the state. Of course, that land had been stolen generations before from Kaskaskia, Mascoutin, Sauk, Miami, Odawa, Peoria, Piankashaw, Wea, Mesquaki, Kickapoo, Potawatomi, Objibwe, and Chickasaw peoples. And of course, that promised education was limited, at least in practice, to white settlers. Though a class in performance history won’t repair the wrongs done to Indigenous peoples in the name of white progress, increasing our knowledge gives us the tools to do better moving forward. We’ll focus on Indigenous performances in North American, beginning with Sor Juana’s The Divine Narcissus, the first play written in an Indigenous language in North America and ending with Neverland, a play yet to premiere (here, in Spring 2021). Along the way, we’ll consider popular Canadian and US “Indian” plays of the 19th C; protest performances such as the Ghost Dance, AIM, and the Keystone Pipeline; the history of exhibiting and archiving Indigenous peoples and performances; and Indigenous tribal and concert dance. Assignments for the class include regular quizzes and performance-as-research group and individual projects. There is no final exam.
